name: TPS2375PW-1
title: TPS2375-1 / TPS2377-1: auto-retry PoE powered-device controllers for IEEE 802.3af
summary: An 8-pin front end for a Power over Ethernet powered device (PD). It presents the 25 kΩ detection signature through an external resistor, draws a classification current set by a second resistor, and, once the input crosses its undervoltage-lockout threshold, connects the load return through an integrated 0.58 Ω, 100 V low-side switch. Start-up current into the bulk capacitor is limited to a level set by a resistor on ILIM, after which a fixed current limit of about 450 mA applies and an open-drain power-good output releases. After a current-limit or thermal fault the part restarts on its own rather than latching off. The TPS2375-1 (TSSOP-8) has 802.3af UVLO thresholds; the TPS2377-1 (SOIC-8) has lower legacy thresholds.

pins.name: ILIM
pins.function: Inrush current programming. A resistor to VSS sets the start-up current limit (Equation 1). Must not be left open or tied straight to VSS; no external voltage may be applied.

pins.name: CLASS
pins.function: Classification programming. A resistor to VSS sets the current drawn while the input is between about 13 V and 21 V, which tells the PSE the PD's class (Table 1). Must not be shorted to ground; no external voltage may be applied.

pins.name: DET
pins.function: Detection. A 24.9 kΩ resistor goes from DET to VDD. DET pulls low while VDD is between 1.4 V and 11.3 V, placing the resistor across the input, and goes open-drain above that range.

pins.name: VSS
pins.function: Negative input rail from the rectified PSE supply; the local ground of the controller. Of all eight pins it couples heat best from the die.

pins.name: RTN
pins.function: Switched negative rail for the downstream load, the drain of the internal pass MOSFET. Inrush and operating current limits act on the current into this pin; PG is referred to it. When VDD-to-RTN is powered from elsewhere and no PoE input is present, the body diode of the MOSFET clamps VSS to RTN.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power good, open-drain, active high, referred to RTN. Released once the pass switch is on and inrush limiting has ended; pulled to RTN otherwise (except in detection). Its pull-down is guaranteed only when VDD sits 4 V or more above RTN. May be left open.

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Positive input rail from the rectified PSE supply, shared with the downstream load. Powers the controller and is the voltage it watches to choose its operating state.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit (Class 3 PD)
circuits.description: A complete 802.3af powered-device front end. Power arrives either on the centre taps of the two data transformers or on the two spare pairs of the RJ-45, in either polarity; two DF01S bridges steer whichever pair is live onto a VDD/VSS rail. Across that rail sit the 0.1 µF input capacitor and an SMAJ58A transient suppressor. R(DET) gives the 25 kΩ detection signature, R(CLASS) = 357 Ω selects Class 3, and R(ILIM) = 178 kΩ sets the inrush current to about 140 mA. The switched return RTN, together with VDD, feeds the DC/DC converter, with a 47 µF bulk capacitor across the output and an optional 100 kΩ pull-up from PG to VDD.

operation.text: An 802.3af supply (PSE) leaves the cable unpowered until it finds a valid PD. It first probes with low voltage (detection), may then ask for the PD's power class (classification), and finally applies full power. While powered, the PD must keep drawing a maintain power signature; if that disappears the PSE removes power and returns to detection. Cable loss is reckoned with 20 Ω of loop resistance: 15.4 W leaves the PSE but only 12.95 W is guaranteed at the PD input. The PSE may feed either the data pairs or the spare pairs, in either polarity, never both, so the PD rectifies both paths with diode bridges; the controller's thresholds carry a 1.5 V offset from the standard's limits to allow for the bridge drop. The PSE limits current to 350–400 mA in normal operation and cuts the PD off if that limit lasts beyond 75 ms.

As VDD rises the controller moves from detection (from 1.4 V) to classification (above V(CL_ON), about 11.3 V), to an idle band above V(CU_OFF) (about 21.9 V) in which DET, CLASS, PG and RTN are all high impedance, and to powered operation above V(UVLO_R). Each comparator has hysteresis.

Below the lower classification threshold the controller draws only minimal bias, holds PG and RTN at high impedance, disables ILIM and CLASS, and pulls DET low so that current through R(DET) forms the signature. A 24.9 kΩ, 1% resistor suits most designs; it dissipates only about 5 mW, so a small part will do. Above 11.3 V DET turns open-drain to save power. The bridge diodes add series resistance at the low detection currents, which can reach hundreds of ohms at 2.7 V, so R(DET) can be trimmed downward for a given diode.

The PSE applies 14.5–20.5 V and measures the current, which is the bias current plus the current set by R(CLASS); the controller draws it while the input lies between 13 V and 21 V and disconnects R(CLASS) above that range. R(CLASS) is chosen from Table 1 for the PD's average power. Its power rating must cover 10 V across it for the 75 ms classification period; on a bench or with an auxiliary supply in this range classification can last much longer, and while thermal shutdown may end it after more than 75 ms, the resistor must not depend on that.

The standard requires a PD to turn on by 42 V and stay on down to 30 V; with a 44 V minimum PSE output and an 8 V cable drop (20 Ω at 400 mA), the PD must work down to 36 V. TPS2375-1 meets those limits. TPS2377-1 turns on lower and with less hysteresis to suit legacy PSEs whose output falls short of 44 V; it also works with compliant PSEs but may start unstably if the PSE output rises slowly, so TPS2375-1 is the choice where PSEs are compliant.

With VDD under the lower UVLO threshold, the current-limit logic sits in reset and RTN floats at high impedance, drifting up to VDD once the output capacitor has discharged. When VDD crosses the turn-on threshold the pass MOSFET turns on with its limit set by R(ILIM); the bulk capacitor charges and RTN falls to near VSS. When the current has stayed about 10% under the programmed limit for 150 µs, the limit steps to the 450 mA operating level and PG opens. The minimum operating limit, 405 mA, sits above the PSE's 400 mA maximum so the PD can use all available power. Inrush limiting keeps start-up under the standard's 400 mA for 50 ms, allows any size of bulk capacitor, and suits legacy PSEs that cannot take large surges. About 140 mA (178 kΩ) is advised for most designs, and below 250 mA where possible, since a lower level also cuts peak stress into an output short.

The downstream converter must not draw more than the inrush limit while that limit is active, or the PD never finishes starting. Enabling the converter from PG, delaying its start until inrush ends, or raising the inrush limit each avoids this; PG is the most reliable of the three.

An overload that drives the switch into current limit with less than 10 V across it (RTN to VSS) lets the bulk capacitor recharge and operation recover if it is brief. If it persists, dissipation of up to 4.5 W can trip thermal shutdown: the MOSFET switches off, with PG low, until the die has cooled. If V(RTN-VSS) is still under 10 V on restart, the 450 mA limit stays and PG opens; if it has risen above 10 V while off, the inrush limit is used and PG stays low, so a PG-controlled converter goes through a normal start.

If the switch is in current limit with more than 10 V across it for 150 µs, the limit drops to the inrush level and PG goes low, lowering stress on the controller, the rest of the PD and the PSE; the peak dissipation then depends on the programmed inrush current. A persistent fault makes the part thermally cycle; when the fault clears the bulk capacitor recharges through a normal start. A fast rise in input voltage also forces current limit while the capacitor charges up to the new level; with a heavy load and a large capacitor this can reach thermal limit, and above 10 V across the switch the limit falls back to the inrush value.

TPS2375-1 never latches off: it relies on current limit, thermal shutdown and foldback to the inrush level, and restarts by itself once a load fault clears or after a source dropout. The latching TPS2375 shuts off after eight over-temperature cycles, or after more than 10 V across the pass switch for 150 µs. A PSE with dc MPS sees a latched PD as removed and recycles power; one with ac MPS may keep powering it. A PD that keeps cycling looks present to both kinds of PSE, so the PSE gets no sign of a fault.
The PSE removes power after 300 ms or more without a valid MPS, which needs at least 10 mA of draw and an ac impedance under 26.25 kΩ in parallel with 0.05 µF.

PG opens roughly 150 µs once the start-up current has dropped 10% under its regulated value, and is held low to RTN while the MOSFET is off, during inrush limiting, or when RTN rises above 10 V. Pull-down is only guaranteed with more than 4 V from VDD to RTN. Because PG is referred to RTN rather than VSS it connects directly to a converter referred to RTN; a pull-up to VDD may not suit every converter. The output is a 100 V open-drain transistor that sinks 2 mA below 0.4 V, and may be left open when unused.

Long inrush limiting, prolonged classification or high ambient can overheat the die. At about 140°C the controller turns off RTN and CLASS, and it restarts when the die has cooled by about 20°C. Thermal protection is active in every state except detection. Many PSEs keep powering a PD shorted beyond the controller, because the MPS is still met, so the part keeps cycling; short spells do not significantly affect reliability but long ones may, and other parts in the power path can also be overstressed. The latching TPS2375 suits parts that cannot tolerate repeated overstress.

A converter draws constant power, so more current at low voltage, and often 25% or more above rated power while starting. The guidelines are: set a moderate inrush current; hold the converter off during inrush; give the converter a soft start that keeps peak start-up input current under 400 mA, ideally only a little above its operating current, from a 44 V source through a 20 Ω loop; failing that, size the bulk capacitor so it sags no more than 8 V while the converter starts from a 400 mA-limited 44 V source through 20 Ω, with start-up finished within 50 ms.

A wall adapter can be diode-ORed in at three points. Option 1, at the converter output, suits adding PoE to a design that already uses a low-voltage adapter; it needs two regulators, the adapter output may be grounded with an isolated converter, and PoE takes priority if its output is set higher. Option 2, across the controller output (VDD to RTN), lets the adapter voltage be below the UVLO; a bulk capacitor of about 22 µF right at the output controls plug-in transients, and an optional series diode at VDD lets the PSE detect and power the PD while the adapter is present, at the cost of its drop. With a low-voltage adapter and automatic PoE priority the inrush limit must exceed the converter's input current at its lowest voltage, and PG is hard to use. Option 3, at the controller input, needs the adapter to exceed the UVLO turn-on and stay under 57 V; PG remains valid and priority goes to the higher voltage, but transients are worst because the node has little capacitance, and an adapter applied first stops the PSE detecting the PD. For options 2 and 3 the adapter needs 1500 Vac dielectric withstand from its ac input and from ground.

The typical application circuit was surged to EN61000-4-2 at 8 kV contact and 15 kV air discharge, between the RJ-45 and the dc outputs and between an auxiliary input jack and the dc outputs, without failure. This covers the controller only, not a finished unit.

The Ethernet isolation transformer needs a centre tap on the cable side, proper termination, and a rating for both the Ethernet chipset and 802.3af. Two full-wave bridges accept power on either pair set in either polarity; silicon p-n diodes rated 1 A or 1.5 A with at least 100 V breakdown suit, their forward drop must stay under 1.5 V at 500 µA at the lowest operating temperature, and their behaviour at detection currents should be tested.

The standard requires 0.05–0.12 µF across the PD input during detection; a 100 V, 10%, X7R ceramic placed next to the controller meets it over temperature. The load capacitance must be at least 5 µF; the controller can charge more than 470 µF before heating becomes a problem, but too large a value can break the MPS when the input dips (Equation 2). Use at least 1 µF directly at the controller output if filtering keeps the bulk capacitor away from it, and about 22 µF there with ORing option 2.

VDD and RTN are rated 100 V absolute maximum from VSS. Plugging and unplugging, ESD, output filters and local power sources can all exceed that, so a TVS such as the SMAJ58A goes after the bridge across the controller input, and enough output capacitance limits ringing from downstream filters.

Place parts along the power flow: RJ-45, Ethernet transformer, bridges, TVS and 0.1 µF capacitor, controller, output capacitor, with no signal crossing from one stage to another. Keep leads short, power traces wide, and each signal paired with its return. Keep safety spacing (for example IEC60950) between the 48 V rails and between input and an isolated converter output. Put the controller over a local plane or fill tied to VSS, use large pads on dissipating parts such as the diodes and the controller, and add copper on the local power and ground nets to spread heat; pin 4 (VSS) is the best heat path out of the die.
